1.pericope_label: If thou wilt return, O Israel, saith the Lord, return unto me: and if thou wilt put away thine abominations out of my sight, then shalt thou not remove
outliers: Calvin sets out three ways of dividing the opening clauses, prefers the one that makes the promise a rest in God, and wholly rejects as forced the rendering, if thou wilt return to me, thou shalt rest
Ellicott reads the closing words of the first verse not as a promise but as a further condition, if thou wilt not wander, where Clarke takes them for a promise of exemption from captivity
themes: A promise answered and then tested
Idols put away out of a sight nothing escapes
An oath treated as though it were an expiation
A blessing the heathen learn to pronounce

3.pericope_label: For thus saith the Lord to the men of Judah and Jerusalem, Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns
outliers: Ellicott hears in the warning against sowing among thorns the germ of a later parable, where likewise the seed is the word of God and the thorns are what chokes it
Calvin presses the wording, that they were not to sow a land once ploughed but to plough it a second time, since a people hardened in their vices needed an unusual and by no means common cultivation
themes: Ground that is ours but lying common
A field sown before it is cleared
A rite that was a boast before men only
A fire that no one can quench

5.pericope_label: Declare ye in Judah, and publish in Jerusalem; and say, Blow ye the trumpet in the land: cry, gather together, and say, Assemble yourselves, and let us go into the defenced cities
debates: Whether the trumpet is a command or a taunt
How retire and stay not should be read
outliers: Calvin denies that the prophet is commanding the alarm at all and reads it as a taunt that shows what the people will do when the distress comes, distinguishing it from an earlier prophet who sounded a trumpet to call men to repent
Gill insists the standard is raised not to enlist soldiers for fighting but only as a sign of danger and a direction where to flee
themes: A herald sent ahead of an army
A banner raised to point the way out
The able going in and the weak going away
A wrath that has not turned aside

7.pericope_label: The lion is come up from his thicket, and the destroyer of the Gentiles is on his way; he is gone forth from his place to make thy land desolate
debates: Why the past tense is used
outliers: Ellicott notes that the word rendered Gentiles answers the sense but has no particular reason to stand here rather than nations, and calls the picture of a land without an inhabitant probably hyperbolical in some measure, though the depopulation was extreme in fact
Calvin denies that the call to mourn is yet a call to repent, and reads it only as notice that a grievous mourning is at hand
themes: A lion coming out of a tangled wood
A prediction told in the past tense
A march begun before the news arrives
A wrath no perverseness will turn aside

9.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass at that day, saith the Lord, that the heart of the king shall perish, and the heart of the princes; and the priests shall be astonished, and the prophets shall wonder
debates: What the heart is that perishes
Who is speaking in the cry
outliers: Calvin allows that the word heart most commonly means understanding but prefers here the sense of strength or courage, and reads the verse as stripping away the confidence the people placed in their king

Calvin rejects both the reading that puts the complaint in the mouth of the people and the one that makes it an expostulation with God, and takes it for a taunt aimed at the false prophets and at those who wanted them
themes: A king left without the wit to command
Prophets named last because they were the cause
A word of peace with a sword behind it
Flatterers deserved and therefore given

11.pericope_label: At that time shall it be said to this people and to Jerusalem, A dry wind of the high places in the wilderness toward the daughter of my people, not to fan, nor to cleanse
debates: What kind of wind is meant
outliers: Ellicott takes swifter than eagles for a quotation from an older lament, and finds the borrowing all but certain because a second phrase from the same lament appears later in this chapter
Calvin rejects as too strained the reading that puts the wind in the mouth of the people, and holds that God speaks, declaring himself the author of the calamity
themes: A wind that will not stop at the chaff
A physician who has given up healing
Clouds rising in a moment out of a clear sky
A cry breaking in on the prophecy

14.pericope_label: O Jerusalem, wash thine heart from wickedness, that thou mayest be saved. How long shall thy vain thoughts lodge within thee?
debates: Whether repentance is the cause of salvation
Why Dan and Ephraim are named
outliers: Ellicott finds a play on one Hebrew word, so that the affliction announced is the same word as the vain thoughts, the nothingness of destruction answering the nothingness of the idol
Calvin denies that the clause makes repentance the cause of salvation, and holds the prophet is only showing that no one can be safe while carrying on war with God
themes: A heart called a shop and forge
A washing once called impossible
A messenger arriving from each place in turn
Ruin named by the word for the idols

16.pericope_label: Make ye mention to the nations; behold, publish against Jerusalem, that watchers come from a far country, and give out their voice against the cities of Judah
debates: Whom the proclamation is addressed to
What the keepers of a field are
outliers: Calvin sets aside two readings of the opening command and takes the prophet to be turning away from a people who would not hear, so that the vengeance is published to the heathen rather than to the Jews
Ellicott notes that the Hebrew word rendered wickedness, like the English word evil, covers both the guilt and its punishment, so that the sentence is that she is reaping her own doing
themes: A ruin announced to strangers because the city will not hear
Guards set round a field of ripe corn
Every road out of the country closed
A bitterness men would rather blame on fortune

19.pericope_label: My bowels, my bowels! I am pained at my very heart; my heart maketh a noise in me; I cannot hold my peace, because thou hast heard, O my soul, the sound of the trumpet, the alarm of war
debates: Why the prophet uses such figures
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch reject a translation that makes it wound meeting wound, since the word means the fracture of a limb and the verb cannot bear the sense of meeting alongside it
Calvin doubts that the prophet is grieving here at all, and takes the outcry for figurative language meant to rouse a torpid people, noting that he laments in the same way over the ruin of enemies
themes: A man in agony who is perfectly well
Bowels taken for the seat of every strong feeling
One crash reported before the last is over
A trumpet that will not stop sounding

22.pericope_label: For my people is foolish, they have not known me; they are sottish children, and they have none understanding: they are wise to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge
debates: What the words of the creation account mean
outliers: Calvin holds the first of the two creation words means emptiness rather than formlessness, and calls the familiar rendering without form improper, since applied to the earth it imports a land unfurnished with produce or inhabitants
Gill limits the earth of the vision to the land of Judea and not the whole world
themes: A people chosen to be lamps and gone dark
Wisdom defined as the fear of God
Four looks in four directions
A land thrown back before the first light

24.pericope_label: I beheld the mountains, and, lo, they trembled, and all the hills moved lightly. I beheld, and, lo, there was no man, and all the birds of the heavens were fled
debates: Why mountains and hills are named
outliers: Calvin argues that Carmel here is the place and not merely a fruitful region, since the next clause speaks of its cities being demolished, and sets the verse against another prophet who says the desert shall become as Carmel
Clarke alone reads the mountains and hills as princes and rulers rather than as the ground itself
themes: Rocks that seemed past all shaking
A land whose birds have gone elsewhere
A vine-land turned into the old wilderness
A preposition repeated for the heat of it

27.pericope_label: For thus hath the Lord said, The whole land shall be desolate; yet will I not make a full end
debates: Whether the clause is a mitigation or a threat
outliers: Calvin sets aside the common reading that makes the clause a mitigation offered to the faithful, and prefers to take the word for an end, so that God declares he will observe no moderation, though he grants that all the early versions favour the other view
Calvin refuses to read the mourning of the earth as the mourning of its inhabitants, and says those who do much diminish the force of the expression
themes: A ruin stopped short of annihilation
Elements made to personate mourners
A sentence the herald did not invent
Men climbing to the clouds to be safe

30.pericope_label: And when thou art spoiled, what wilt thou do? Though thou clothest thyself with crimson, though thou deckest thee with ornaments of gold, though thou rentest thy face with painting, in vain shalt thou make thyself fair
debates: How the opening words should be read
What the painting of the face was
Why the travail is of a first child
outliers: Calvin reports a textual difficulty in the opening words, the pronoun being feminine while the participle is masculine, and allows a rendering that takes the second word for an infinitive, so that the line runs, and against spoiling what wilt thou do

Calvin rejects as frigid the construction that turns the following clauses into relatives, who now adornest thyself, who clothest thyself in scarlet, since the relative alters the meaning of the prophet
themes: A ruined woman at her mirror
Antimony laid on until the lid nearly tears
A city dressed to charm the army besieging it
Labour beginning in the middle of a meal
